newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Analysts raise oil price forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Analysts raise oil price forecasts.

text.p: Analysts are revising up their oil price forceasts for the fourth quarter now that the Iraqi crisis has put a hold on the return of Iraqi exports oil that buyers were counting on to meet winter heating fuel demand.

Robbed of roughly six months' exports at 550,000 barrels per day of Iraqi crude which had been expected to start flowing this month as part of a United Nations oil-for-food deal, the oil market is facing the winter with low inventories of heating fuel on both sides of the Atlantic.

Given the instabiliy in Iraq and other Middle East oil producers and the possibility of another extremely cold winter, oil prices are expected to remain firm and price volatility is expected to continue.

"Certainly in the fourth quarter we expect there to be some impact because of what's happened in the last few days...We were working on the basis that some Iraqi oil would be on the market," said Colin Birch, consultant at Purvin and Gertz in London.
"Probably more of an impact is next year and the year after where we're likely to be revising the numbers up in that time frame as well," he said.

He expects to raise his previous fourth quarter 1996 and first quarter 1997 price estimates for North Sea crude Brent. Currently those estimates stand at $17 and $15.50, respectively, compared to year-ago averages of $17.11 and $18.56.

The spot Brent crude futures contract on the International Petroleum Exchange soared to $22.85 a barrel on Tuesday, its highest level since $23.30 in April. It eased back to $21.95 at 1220 GMT Thursday but remains well above its late July price of $19.
The September gas oil (heating oil) futures contract jumped to $215.50 a tonne on Tuesday, the highest level for the spot contract since $223 in November 1991.
Gas oil has rallied about $43 or 20 percent since July.

"Just-in-time inventory management, Iraqi uncertainty and the winter weather conditions uncertainty could lead to greater price volatility," said Cyrus Tahmassebi, president of Energy Trends, Inc in Washington.
"(The Iraqi oil sale delay) will certainly have a physical impact and on top of that there is this speculative factor," he said. "There is a fear in the market that things could get out of control."

He raised his target for West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark crude, to $21 in the fourth and first quarters, from a previous estimate of $18-$19. Oct crude on the New York Mercantile Exchange closed Tuesday at $23.24.

Keith Hamm, chairman of Petroleum Economics, Ltd in London, expects Brent to hold in a $19-$21 range during the fourth quarter. He had previously estimated prices to fall through the bottom of that range later this year with the arrival of Iraqi crude.
He said it was too early to accurately predict first quarter prices, but even that was a change of market sentiment.
"Previously that would have been seen as a very weak period with the cumulative impact of Iraqi crude oil plus the seasonal downturn at the end of the first quarter," he said.
"Now we're sitting back to reevaluate to see with Iraqi crude out if the market will be sufficiently balanced."
Analysts expected Iraqi crude output and exports to continue edging higher once it got the go-ahead for the first oil sale.
"Forecasts are under review," said Geoff Pyne, oil economist at UBS in London, who was estimating a $17.50 Brent average in the fourth quarter.
He cautioned it was too early to fix forecasts for 1997.

The U.S. said on Tuesday it could take "months and months" before the May 20 oil-for-food deal worked out between Iraq and the United Nations, which would allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, could go into effect.
Overall trade sanctions, which are separate from the deal, have been in place since shortly after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Analysts were unanimous, though, in forecasting continued steady, not lower, heating oil prices.

Stocks of middle distillate, including heating oil and diesel, are 18 million barrels below year-ago levels in the U.S. at around 109 million barrels. In Europe, as of July, inventories were down 10.5 million from a year ago.
